title: Customer Credit Risk
answer: Customer credit risk is the chance that a buyer will not pay what they owe on the terms agreed, and it covers the whole life of a receivable from the first order through to final settlement. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Customer credit risk is the chance that a buyer will not pay what they owe on the terms agreed, and it covers the whole life of a receivable from the first order through to final settlement. In payables and receivables work it decides who gets credit, how much, on what terms, and how hard the business chases the money afterwards. It sits alongside collections, cash forecasting and bad debt provisioning, and it draws on order history, payment behaviour, financial statements and external credit data.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the accounting and ERP systems that already hold the customer ledger, plus a credit or collections module where limits, terms and dunning status live. Data arrives from bank feeds, remittance files, trade references and credit bureaus, and increasingly from open banking connections that show cash position directly. Models are usually trained and scored outside the ledger, then written back as a limit, a score or a flag that a credit controller can act on. Spreadsheets still carry a great deal of the analysis in smaller finance teams.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts combine rule based checks, such as days beyond terms and limit utilisation, with statistical scoring that weighs payment history, order size, sector and external ratings. Machine learning adds gradient boosted models and, where text is involved, language models that read correspondence, dispute notes and news for early warning signs. Outputs are typically a probability of default or of late payment, a recommended limit, and a ranked list of accounts needing attention. The results are reviewed by a human before a limit changes or an order is held.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Credit decisions touch personal and business data, so lawful basis, retention and fairness in scoring matter, and in some jurisdictions a declined applicant has a right to an explanation. Automated refusals usually need a human review path and a documented reason code. Provenance of external data, bureau scores and model versions should be recorded so a decision can be reconstructed later. Internal policy sets who can override a limit, how disputes are logged, and how provisioning follows accounting standards.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect closer integration between credit scoring and live cash data, so limits adjust as a customer's payment behaviour changes rather than at annual review. Explainable models and audit trails will matter more as regulators look at automated lending and trade credit decisions. Smaller finance teams will get access to scoring that was once only affordable to large corporates, through embedded tools in accounting platforms. The human credit controller is likely to shift from calculating limits to handling exceptions, disputes and relationships.
